description: Nồi cơm điện: a white rice cooker with a flowery lid and a cracked steam vent, the one appliance every Saigon kitchen owns.  Plug it into a live socket and it will heat whatever you put in a pot on it.

Bếp than tổ ong: a squat clay-lined bucket stove built to burn one honeycomb coal briquette at a time.  Poor households, street vendors and every phở cart cook on one.  Set it down to light a contained fire.
Than tổ ong: a cylinder of pressed coal dust punched through with nineteen holes, so it burns slowly and evenly for a couple of hours.  It leaves your hands black.
A dented aluminium phin: a cup-sized drip filter with a perforated press and a lid.  It turns a spoon of robusta into a slow, strong coffee.
A paper packet of dark, oily ground robusta from the Central Highlands, roasted with butter and a little fish sauce the way the cafés like it.
Thick, sickly-sweet condensed milk from a tin with a picture of a bird on it.  A finger of it at the bottom of the glass is what makes cà phê sữa.
A small plastic bag with a straw, tied off with a rubber band: how street vendors sell iced coffee and sugarcane juice to go.  It holds liquid as long as you don't squeeze it.
A ribbed plastic cup with a striped straw stuck through a sealed film lid, from a drinks stall.
A tall glass bottle with a red cap and a fading label showing an anchovy and a fishing boat.
A dented household LPG cylinder, painted red and stencilled with a distributor's phone number.  Every kitchen has one under the counter, chained to a two-burner stove.
A blue 20-litre plastic can with a screw cap, used for drinking water, fish sauce, petrol or anything else that needs carrying home on a motorbike.
